sections.title: Five formats, one renderer
sections.content:
This topic exists to verify that the renderer handles every quiz variant the generator can produce. Below you'll find one quiz of each type — answer them in order to confirm input, feedback, and persistence work.

If anything renders broken, that's the bug to fix before we generate any more courses.

sections.question: Which quiz format is best when you have 4 plausible distractors and want to test applied judgement?
sections.explanation: Multiple choice shines when you have several similar-looking options and want to force the learner to pick the right reasoning. The others all serve narrower purposes — T/F for sharp claims, fill-in for specific values, open-ended for synthesis.

sections.statement: Multiple choice is always the best quiz format because it gives the most options.
sections.explanation: More options isn't automatically better. Fill-in-the-blank tests recall sharper. Matching tests pattern recognition. Open-ended tests synthesis. The right format depends on what you're trying to teach.

sections.question: Match each quiz variant to the situation it fits best.

pairs.right: Pinpoint a specific value or term

sections.explanation: Each format has a sweet spot. Picking the right one for each topic is the whole point of having a library to choose from.

sections.sentence: The standard coffee-to-water ratio for a balanced pour-over brew is ___.
sections.explanation: 1:16 (one gram of coffee per sixteen grams of water) is the widely accepted starting point. From there you adjust based on taste — stronger or weaker. Fill-in-the-blank is perfect when a single specific value is the whole point.

sections.question: If a teammate asked you to recommend which quiz format to use for a topic on giving feedback, what would you say and why?
sections.sample_answer: I'd lean toward open-ended (short-answer) because feedback is a synthesis skill — there's no single right wording. The learner needs to compose a response that balances clarity, care, and specificity. A multiple-choice quiz might test whether they recognise good feedback when they see it, but it doesn't force them to generate it.
key_points: Mention that feedback is a synthesis skill
Note that open-ended forces generation, not just recognition
Acknowledge that MC tests recognition (a different skill)
Connect format choice to the cognitive demand of the topic
sections.explanation: Strong answers connect the quiz format to the cognitive load of the topic, not just to surface features. Recognising vs. generating is the key distinction here.

sections.title: Why variety matters
sections.content: A 20-topic course where every quiz is multiple choice gets monotonous fast — and it under-tests skills like recall, pattern recognition, and synthesis. The generator now distributes variants across topics deliberately so the learner gets a mix.

points: Multiple choice is best when distractors carry real judgement weight.
True/false is best for sharp claims and common misconceptions.
Matching is best for pairing terms with definitions or scenarios with strategies.
Fill-in-the-blank is best when one specific value, name, or phrase is the lesson.
Open-ended is best when synthesis matters more than the exact wording of the answer.

flashcards.front: When is multiple choice the right quiz format?
flashcards.back: When you have 3-4 plausible distractors and want to test applied judgement — picking the best reasoning out of several similar-looking options.

flashcards.front: When is fill-in-the-blank the right quiz format?
flashcards.back: When a single specific value, name, ratio, or short phrase is the actual lesson — and you want the learner to retrieve it from memory, not just recognise it.

flashcards.front: When is open-ended the right quiz format?
flashcards.back: When the concept requires synthesis no fixed answer captures — the learner writes free text, then self-assesses against a sample answer and key points.

flashcards.front: Why distribute quiz variants across topics?
flashcards.back: A course of 20 multiple-choice quizzes gets monotonous and under-tests recall, pattern recognition, and synthesis. Variety keeps engagement up and tests more dimensions of understanding.
